eyebrow: Statistics & Probability for Data Science · Chapter 1, Lesson 2
subtitle: The kind of variable decides which statistics and charts make sense.

steps.label: NUMERICAL: CONTINUOUS
steps.sub: Any value in a range — order value

steps.label: NOMINAL
steps.sub: No order — count it, take the mode

steps.label: ORDINAL
steps.sub: Ordered, unequal gaps — rank, take the median

steps.label: INTERVAL
steps.sub: Equal gaps, no true zero — Celsius

steps.label: RATIO
steps.sub: Equal gaps AND a true zero — order value, weight

code:
df = pd.DataFrame({
  "customer_id": [101, 102, 103, 104, 105],
  "satisfaction": ["low","high","medium","high","medium"]})

df["customer_id"].mean()   # 103.0 -- meaningless; IDs are nominal labels
caption: An int64 ID still means nothing when averaged. satisfaction is just text -- no order, yet.

code:
print(df["region"].value_counts())
# East 2, West 2, North 1  -- counts are the honest nominal summary

cats = ["low", "medium", "high"]
df["satisfaction"] = pd.Categorical(df["satisfaction"], categories=cats, ordered=True)
df["satisfaction"].max()   # 'high'
caption: Ordered categorical: max/min/sort respect the ranking instead of sorting alphabetically.
